headline: July's inflation report lands at 8:30 this morning with the September call a coin flip — a quarter-point hike near 50% — after stocks slipped Tuesday, Brent settled at $88.95, and a second Fed official in two days named inflation the economy's main problem.
stance: The report everyone has been waiting on arrives at 8:30am ET, and the market went into it almost perfectly undecided. Interest-rate futures pricing puts a quarter-point September hike at roughly 50% this morning, down from just over 52% a day earlier — a coin flip, and a long way from the confident hold the market priced after Friday's jobs contraction. Forecasters look for consumer prices to have risen 0.1% in July and 3.4% over the past year, down from 3.5% in June, with the core measure that strips out food and energy up 0.2% on the month and 2.5% on the year. Stocks marked time waiting: the S&P 500 fell 0.32% Tuesday to 7,728.20, the Dow 0.34% to 53,791.85 and the Nasdaq 100 0.33% to 26,445.45. Treasuries firmed a touch — the 10-year yield closed at 4.70% from 4.72% Monday, the 2-year at 4.22% from 4.25% — while Brent settled at $88.95 from $87.85 and traded near $89.61 overnight after fresh attacks on shipping dented hopes the Strait of Hormuz reopens soon. The tension in today's print is simple: the labour market says the Fed is already tight enough, and oil near $90 says the inflation job is not finished.

news.head: The inflation report is today, not tomorrow
news.body: July consumer prices are released at 8:30am ET. Forecasters look for a 0.1% rise on the month and 3.4% over the past year, down from June's 3.5%; the core measure that excludes food and energy is seen up 0.2% on the month and 2.5% on the year. June's 3.5% was itself the mildest reading since March and came in well under the 3.8% economists expected, so the bar for another downside surprise is higher than it was a month ago.

news.head: September is now a coin flip
news.body: Interest-rate futures pricing puts a quarter-point September hike at roughly 50% this morning, down from just over 52% a day earlier. There is one more inflation report between now and the September 15-16 meeting, so today's number sets the lean rather than settling it.

news.head: A second Fed official in two days pointed at inflation
news.body: Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee said Tuesday that "the biggest problem facing our economy right now is not the collapse of industry and the collapse of jobs; it's that the prices have been rising too fast, we got an inflation problem and people hate inflation." He described the job market as "stable, without being good." That follows Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack on Monday. Both of the officials who have spoken since the July payrolls contraction have led with prices, not jobs.

news.head: CoreWeave beat, then raised its spending plan sharply
news.body: The AI-infrastructure company reported second-quarter revenue of $2.58 billion against about $2.56 billion expected, and an adjusted loss of $1.03 a share against a $1.20 loss expected. Its booked order backlog stands at $104 billion. But it lifted this year's capital-spending plan to $35-39 billion from $31-34 billion, and its net loss widened to $626 million from $290 million a year earlier. Third-quarter revenue guidance of $3.4-3.6 billion brackets the roughly $3.43 billion analysts expected. The shares rose in after-hours trading on the report and were up about 2.4% pre-market (~5am ET).

news.head: Attacks on shipping pushed oil back toward $90
news.body: Brent settled Tuesday at $88.95, up from $87.85 Monday, and traded at $89.61 overnight. Yemen's government accused Iran-aligned Houthis of killing six people in missile attacks on a commercial vessel in the Bab al-Mandeb strait on Tuesday, and US Central Command disabled a cargo vessel trying to breach the blockade of Iranian ports. Qatar's foreign ministry said talks between Oman and Iran were "at an advanced stage," while Iran maintains the strait stays closed until sanctions are lifted and war reparations paid. Ten vessels crossed the Strait of Hormuz on Monday, against roughly 130 a day before the war.

news.head: Tuesday's insider filings brought back a multi-buyer cluster
news.body: Filings dated Tuesday show about $8.8 million bought at BRVE across 13 separate filings by ten different insiders — the widest group purchase in the current run of filings — plus $4.3 million at LITB from a single buyer. The largest single-name figure in the current filings is still Monday's roughly $10.1 million at LOCL, but that was one insider acting alone.

implications: Today's print decides the lean, not the decision. With hike odds at roughly 50% and one more inflation report due before the September meeting, a 0.1% monthly reading in line with forecasts leaves the argument exactly where it is; the number that moves it is one showing energy costs feeding through to the rest of the basket while Brent sits near $90.

The bond market spent Tuesday leaning the other way to the Fed speakers. The 10-year yield fell to 4.70% from 4.72% and the 10-year breakeven — the inflation rate bond prices imply over the next decade — eased to 2.27% from 2.29%, even as two officials named inflation the main problem. The inflation-adjusted 10-year yield was unchanged at 2.43%, so this was a repricing of expected inflation rather than of growth.

Hedging into the print happened in bonds, not stocks. The MOVE index, the Treasury market's equivalent of the VIX, rose to 77.9 from 75.5 — a second straight increase — while the VIX fell to 15.28 from 15.46 and its Nasdaq counterpart to 22.38 from 23.04. Equity protection is cheap going into a two-sided event, which cuts both ways: little is priced for a shock, and little has been spent guarding against one.

CoreWeave's spending raise is the part with reach beyond one stock. Lifting capital spending to $35-39 billion from $31-34 billion is a demand signal for the chip, power and construction supply chain, and a reminder that AI revenue growth is being bought with cash today. Cisco reports after today's close into the same question.

watch.head: Consumer prices, 8:30am ET
watch.body: Forecasts centre on +0.1% for the month and 3.4% over the past year, with core at +0.2% and 2.5%. Read the energy and services detail rather than the headline: with Brent near $90, whether higher fuel costs are showing up in airfares, shipping and other services is what tells you if this is a passing energy bump or something the Fed has to answer.

watch.head: Cisco after today's close
watch.body: The networking company reports fiscal fourth-quarter results after the market closes; analysts expect about $1.17 a share. Coming the day after CoreWeave lifted its spending plan, the read of interest is what Cisco says about orders from data-centre customers — the same AI build-out, seen from the equipment side.

watch.head: Whether the strait actually reopens
watch.body: Qatar calls the Oman-Iran talks "advanced"; Iran says the closure holds until sanctions relief and reparations; ten vessels crossed on Monday against roughly 130 a day before the war. Transit counts recovering, or a published agreement, are what would settle this. Statements alone have moved Brent from $82 to near $90 in four sessions and can move it back just as fast.

watch.head: Whether the coin flip breaks
watch.body: Hike odds sit at roughly 50% this morning, down from just over 52% a day earlier. Watch where they sit an hour after the print — that reaction, more than the number itself, tells you which of the two competing stories the market has decided to run with into September.

sections.title: Macro & Rates
bullets: The biggest change since yesterday morning: the inflation report is no longer ahead of the market, it is here — 8:30am ET — and September has settled into a coin flip. Interest-rate futures pricing puts a quarter-point hike at roughly 50%, down from just over 52% a day earlier. Forecasts look for prices up 0.1% on the month and 3.4% over the past year, from 3.5% in June, with core at 0.2% and 2.5%.

A second official in two days led with prices. Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee said Tuesday that "the biggest problem facing our economy right now is not the collapse of industry and the collapse of jobs; it's that the prices have been rising too fast," and called the job market "stable, without being good" — following Cleveland's Beth Hammack on Monday.

Treasuries firmed slightly against that: the 10-year yield closed Tuesday at 4.70% from 4.72% Monday, the 2-year at 4.22% from 4.25%, with the gap between them at +48 basis points. The 10-year breakeven — the annual inflation rate bond prices imply over the next ten years — eased to 2.27% from 2.29%, while the inflation-adjusted 10-year yield held at 2.43%.

Oil stayed the complicating factor. Brent settled at $88.95 from $87.85 Monday and traded at $89.61 overnight after Yemen's government accused Houthi forces of a deadly missile attack on a commercial vessel in the Bab al-Mandeb strait and US Central Command disabled a cargo ship running the blockade of Iranian ports. Ten vessels crossed Hormuz on Monday against roughly 130 a day before the war. US crude settled at $83.23 from $82.30.

Elsewhere in the prior close: gold eased to $4,427.80 from $4,448.60 and silver to $64.86 from $65.88, both giving back a little of Monday's push. The dollar index sat at 99.82 and the yen at ¥159.24, essentially unchanged from Monday's ¥159.22 and still at the weak end of its three-year range. July existing-home sales, released Tuesday, fell 1.7% on the month to 4.06 million, close to the 4.05 million expected.
sections.positioning: New in the latest weekly futures data: speculators flipped to an extended short position in 10-year Treasury futures — the 12th percentile of the past three years, down 17 percentile points in a week — a contrarian-bullish lean for bond prices going into today's print. Speculators also moved to an extended long in the dollar index, at the 90th percentile and up 13 points on the week, with hedgers at the opposite extreme.

sections.title: Equity Markets
bullets: Tuesday's close: the S&P 500 fell 0.32% to 7,728.20, the Dow 0.34% to 53,791.85 and the Nasdaq 100 0.33% to 26,445.45 — a second straight decline, leaving the index below Friday's record close. Overnight (~5am ET), S&P 500 futures were about 0.2% higher and Dow futures roughly flat, with Nasdaq futures the firmer of the three.

CoreWeave reported after Tuesday's close: revenue of $2.58 billion against about $2.56 billion expected and an adjusted loss of $1.03 a share against a $1.20 loss expected, with a booked order backlog of $104 billion. The company raised this year's capital-spending plan to $35-39 billion from $31-34 billion and guided third-quarter revenue to $3.4-3.6 billion, bracketing the roughly $3.43 billion expected. Its net loss widened to $626 million from $290 million a year earlier. The shares rose in after-hours trading and were up about 2.4% pre-market (~5am ET).
Cisco reports after today's close, with analysts looking for about $1.17 a share — the same AI build-out question CoreWeave just answered, from the equipment supplier's side.

Protection stayed cheap into the print: the VIX closed Tuesday at 15.28, down from 15.46 Monday, and its Nasdaq-100 counterpart at 22.38 from 23.04. The skew index, which measures what investors pay for insurance against a large drop, sat at 135.6.

Breadth barely moved: 64.9% of S&P 500 members closed above their 50-day trend line, from 65.3% Monday, and 55% of Nasdaq-100 members did, unchanged. On the longer 200-day measure it is 72.5% and 73% respectively — participation is broad, it is conviction that is thin.
sections.positioning: Standing background rather than a new development: bullish bets in Nasdaq 100 futures remain at the 1st percentile of the past three years and Russell 2000 futures at the 2nd, with hedgers at the opposite extreme in both — scepticism, not exuberance, underneath a tape near its highs.

single_name.note: (Lineage, the largest owner of temperature-controlled warehouses — the cold storage food companies rent) — an insider purchase was filed Monday, the shares trade above their 200-day trend line, and the scan's dark-pool and options signals are both live. At 7.5 days of average trading volume, it also carries the heaviest short position on the current list, which cuts both ways if the shares keep rising.

sections.title: Credit & Liquidity
bullets: Credit stayed unbothered by the oil move through the latest available data, which runs a day behind: the extra yield high-yield bonds pay over investment-grade was 270 basis points in Monday's data, unchanged from Friday, with investment-grade spreads at 78 basis points.

The hedging ahead of today's report went into bonds rather than stocks. The MOVE index — the Treasury market's version of the VIX — rose to 77.9 from 75.5 Monday, a second straight increase, while the VIX fell.
Short-term funding stayed quiet: the key bank-funding spreads sat at zero and the commercial-paper funding spread at 21 basis points in the latest readings, with no sign of stress in the plumbing.

The system's spare-cash cushion is still effectively gone: the Fed's overnight reverse-repo facility held $1.2 billion Tuesday, against bank reserves of $2,993.3 billion and $907.3 billion in the Treasury's cash account in last Wednesday's weekly snapshot.
sections.positioning: Primary-dealer high-yield inventory remains mid-range — the 35th percentile of its three-year span, unchanged — with no positioning extreme flagged anywhere in the credit book this week.
